purpose: This medication helps your body make more white blood cells, which are the cells that fight infections. It is used to lower your risk of getting serious infections after chemotherapy, which can reduce your white blood cell count. Keeping your white blood cell count up helps protect you while you are going through cancer treatment.
how_it_works: Your bone marrow is like a factory that makes blood cells. Chemotherapy can slow down that factory, leaving you with fewer infection-fighting white blood cells. This medicine sends a signal to your bone marrow to speed up and make more white blood cells so your body can better defend itself against germs.
common_side_effects: Bone pain or achiness (especially in the back, hips, or legs) is the most common side effect. You may also notice mild redness, swelling, or bruising at the injection site. Some people feel tired, have headaches, or experience mild muscle aches.
warnings: Rarely, this medicine can cause a serious condition where your spleen enlarges and could rupture — call your doctor right away if you have sudden sharp pain in your upper left belly or left shoulder. It can also cause a serious lung reaction (ARDS), so tell your doctor if you have trouble breathing, fever, or cough. Do not use this medication between 14 days before and 24 hours after receiving chemotherapy. People with sickle cell disease should use this medicine with caution.
typical_dosing: It is usually given as a single injection under the skin (subcutaneous) once per chemotherapy cycle, typically about 24 hours after your chemotherapy is finished. Your doctor or nurse will give you the injection, or you may be shown how to give it at home. Each dose is 6 mg regardless of your body weight.
